intro: The Battle of Brandywine was fought around this sycamore on 11 September 1777, when it was already 168 years old by the reckoning of the college that later raised a seedling from its seed. It stands beside the Gideon Gilpin farmhouse, where the wounded Marquis de Lafayette had his leg dressed that day. Five and a half metres round and thirty-four metres tall, with the flaking white upper limbs American sycamores show once the leaves are down. The battlefield grounds are free to walk and the tree is a short way in.
meta_description: This sycamore was already 168 years old when the Battle of Brandywine was fought around it in 1777. It still stands by the Gilpin farmhouse.
question_meta: The Brandywine Sycamore, about 400 years old, stands beside the Gideon Gilpin House at Brandywine Battlefield Park in Chadds Ford, PA.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Chadds Ford is the Brandywine Sycamore, also called the Lafayette Sycamore, an American sycamore of roughly 400 years standing beside the Gideon Gilpin House in Brandywine Battlefield Park, off Baltimore Pike. Union County College, which grew a seedling from its seed in 1997, records the parent as dating from about 1609 and measuring 220 inches around and 111 feet tall, which made it 168 years old on the day of the battle in 1777. The farmhouse it stands beside is where the Marquis de Lafayette, shot through the leg, was taken to be treated. A 1987 bicentennial marker sits at its foot. The park grounds are free to walk; the house interior is seen on timed guided tours only.
question_context: Brandywine Battlefield Park is off Baltimore Pike in Chadds Ford, roughly 40 km from central Philadelphia and about an hour by road. There is no public transport to it, so this is a car trip. The grounds are free to walk and the tree stands outside the Gideon Gilpin house, so seeing it costs nothing and takes minutes. The house interior is a different matter: timed guided tours only, Thursday to Sunday, so check the park's hours before you build a day around it. The battlefield is a National Historic Landmark covering the fighting of 11 September 1777, and the Gilpin farmhouse is where Lafayette was brought after a musket ball went through his leg. The sycamore beside it was, on Union County College's record, already 168 years old that afternoon. A bicentennial marker placed in 1987 stands at its base. The coordinates here mark the house rather than the trunk, because no tree-level fix has been published, but the two stand a yard apart, so nothing about that will cost you a search.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Chadds Ford?
faq.a: The Brandywine Sycamore, beside the Gideon Gilpin House at Brandywine Battlefield Park. It dates from about 1609 on the record of the college that propagated it, which makes it roughly 400 years old.

faq.q: Did this tree really witness the Battle of Brandywine?
faq.a: It was standing here and it was old enough. The battle was fought across these fields on 11 September 1777 and the tree was about 168 years old at the time, beside the farmhouse where Lafayette was treated. Nothing in the wood records the fighting; the claim rests on its age and its position, and both are documented.

faq.q: Is it free, and can I walk up to it?
faq.a: Yes. The park grounds are free and the tree stands in the open beside the house. Only the house interior is ticketed, on timed guided tours Thursday to Sunday.

faq.q: When is the best time to see it?
faq.a: January and February, when the leaves are down and the white upper limbs show, which is what a sycamore of this size does best. Summer gives you the shade and the 60-foot limb spread instead.

On 11 September 1777 the fighting ran through these fields, and the Marquis de Lafayette, nineteen years old and shot through the leg, was carried into the Gideon Gilpin farmhouse the tree stands beside to have the wound dressed. A bicentennial marker went in beside it in 1987. Worth saying plainly what a witness tree is and is not. Nothing in the wood records the battle.
